utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Licina. I believe you already know it by now but that notwithstanding it's still my duty to remind you once again that you are still bound by the oath -- beg your pardon, the declaration you made at the beginning to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you did indicate yesterday that you have no questions for the witness. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Thank you. I know the witness has to catch a plane so I'll try to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Licina, just a couple of questions arising from the questions that were asked of you yesterday by His Honour Judge Moloto and His Honour Judge Hoepfel. You were asked about your view that the Serb nation within Croatia had a right to self-determination. Do you remember that topic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say that the Serb nation has a right to self-determination, you're talking about Serbs as an ethnic group, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And the same is true for Croats, it's the Croats as an ethnic group that you say you also recognise their right to self-determination? You nodded. I think you have to say yes, if you heard the question.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpretation to finish. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So my question for you is: What -- under your view of things, what happens to the Croats who live in Serb areas of Croatia, such as in parts of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Croats in Krajina, in fact, Krajina had 88 per cent of Serb population. Our intention was that in case of dissolution, in case of secession, both people should have a public vote and Croatia as such should be re-composed. But that was all up -- subject to negotiations. Croats would in that case have all their civic rights within Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But wasn't that the case of Serbs in Croatia, that they had all their civic rights, those -- all civic rights were guaranteed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Serbs in Croatia do you mean? You mean all of them or generally or do you mean those that would remain as a minority?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Both. Under the 1990 constitution, the new constitution, all the rights of minorities were guaranteed, right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are two different concepts. Croatia was not defined in terms of constitution as a state of citizens so it was -- it was a matter of concept, of design.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I guess my point is --

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was defined as an ethnic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My point is, under your view, Croats living in the Krajina, they would have no other way to exercise their right to self-determination. They would just simply be guaranteed ordinary civic rights. That's what you're saying would happen to the Croats in Krajina and what I'm putting to you is, that's the same situation as the Serbs in Croatia, right? You were guaranteed your civic rights.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia as one of the republics was created by agreement of two peoples, the Croatian and the Serbian people. Both peoples had confirmed their wish to live within that state. If the status of that state was about to change, then both peoples should have been asked for their agreement, whereas in reality what occurred is that one people, one of the two peoples, was reduced to the status of national minority. If it had been a state of citizens, a civic state, if that was what Croatia had been, then your question would make sense but otherwise, no. Serbia, for instance, has a formulation in its constitution that Serbia is a state of the citizens of Serbia. That is what is written in the Serbian constitution now, and that was the case even before, in fact, from 1990 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that's also what the Croatian constitution says, right? It says it's a state of the Croat people and then all the other citizens of Croatia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What is written is that it is a state of the Croat people. That is the essential difference. The essential difference is that the Croatia is a state of the Croat people. If Croatia were a state of the citizens of Croatia, that would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't want to ask too many more questions about this because I think we go around in circles but isn't it right that as soon as you focus on ethnic groups as the holders of this right of self-determination, that inevitably leads to ethnic separation, that the Croats, Croatians going to -- Croats go to Croatia, the Serbs come into SAO Krajina, then the Croat communities within Serb Krajina have to form their own views; it's just this spiral of ethnic separation; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not an ethnic separation. That state had been created in the first place by agreement of two peoples and that was the original formulation in the constitution, that it was a state of two peoples. Nowadays, it's only a state of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. But once the Croatian republic separated from Yugoslavia, Yugoslavia dissolved, and once that happened then you're saying that the ethnic Serbs in Krajina had this right of self-determination so they could separate themselves from Croatia. And I'm saying that once you go down that path, it's just an inevitable path of ethnic separation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, the dissolution of Yugoslavia, too, leads to ethnic separation. It's exactly the same concept. Why, then, did we have to break up Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the Badinter Commission, which operated at the beginning of 1992? Are you familiar with that name?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know that in January of 1992, the Badinter Commission concluded that Serbs in Croatia were entitled to protection of every minority right under international law?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that but I don't think it is fair. I don't think it's correct. I cannot go any more deeply into this subject because I'm not an expert, but Serbs considered the decision of the Badinter Commission very detrimental and very wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that was probably also because the Badinter Commission went a little further and said that the right to self-determination could not include a right to change borders or frontiers. Did you also hear about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With that decision, the Badinter Commission started to interfere with the law as it was written then. The law of Yugoslavia at the time spoke of the sovereignty of peoples, not republics, and that is the essence of the conflict within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thanks for your patience, Mr. Licina. No more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Licina, this brings us to the end of your testimony. We thank you very much for coming to testify at the Tribunal notwithstanding what I believe should be a very busy schedule. You are now excused. You may stand down. Once again, thank you very much for coming to testify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just ask your permission to say hello to Mr. Martic, if that's not a problem? I haven't seen him for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem is you can't say it now in court unless you're prepared to wait and see him after court, during the break. But right now it's not going to be possible. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can wait until the first break, if I have your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. You don't have my permission. You'll have to ask from security [Realtime transcript read in error, "skut"]. If they agree, that will be fine. I don't have the power to give you that authority. Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see they say the transcript shows that I said he will have to ask from skut. I said he will have to ask from security. Okay. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. May I ask that the next Defence witness be brought into the courtroom? I don't know if I can pronounce his name right now or is what I have already said sufficient? Because of the protective measures. I have no experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What you have already said is sufficient, Mr. Milovancevic. Don't mention his name, precisely for that reason. I guess the person who brings the witness knows who to bring without the name having to be announced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session? I'm aware that when the witness came in we were already in private session but we are back in open session. May we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In the town where you used to work and live, what was the ethnic structure of the population, without mentioning the name place, and what was your situation at work in that sense?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town where I started working in the service for internal affairs, it's a town of about 250.000, the population being mainly mixed, with just a slight majority of ethnic Croats, but there was also a large number of Serbs, Muslims and others. The town was culturally and industrially developed, it had its own university, various industries, including the military industry, a lot of military personnel, and at my workplace, Serbs and Croats were half/half, and there were some employees of Muslim faith and Muslim ethnicity. The atmosphere was harmonious in the town in general, without any major incidents, or major conflicts, along ethnic lines, because at that time we had a legal system and services that combatted all such incidents and penalised them very harshly with 30 days' imprisonment. As for relations within the police, relations were harmonious, nobody insulted anybody. There were no ethnic slurs. And that was most strictly prohibited. Sometimes in town, there occurred incidents, especially when football and basketball teams from Belgrade and Serbia would come to visit, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, you said that there were incidents when the clubs would meet. Such incidents are common throughout Europe. You said that they were severely punished here. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was severely punished because at the time it was known and it was assumed that the small incidents, which were of an ethnic cause, could cause further conflicts among citizens, not just between the police and not just between the police and citizens but could cause mutual conflicts among citizens of different ethnic groups, that's why such rigorous punishment was applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Regarding what you said about these sports events, did anyone, fans, come from outside to the place where you worked and what happened on such occasions?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many fans would come with the particular club, for example fans would come from Belgrade, if the club was from Belgrade. These would be also the matches would be attended by ethnic Serbs from different towns in Croatia, towns around Sibenik and in other places, fans originating from Serbia, who rooted for those clubs. Then they would experience different unpleasant things at the stadium, the police would prevent such excesses at the stadium but on their way to the stadium and from the stadium, most often they used trains to get there, that's when incidents would occur. They would be attacked in trains, the trains would be stoned, things would be broken, insults hurled. This was specific particularly for the region of Zagora. I don't want to mention the specific locations but there were specific locations where the trains carrying the fans from Belgrade would be stoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said that this was rigorously punished and prevented so that such incidents would not turn into larger clashes. As for maintaining public peace and order, was that something that was also under control?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was under control because the police forces were united regardless of whether they were Serbs or Croats. All of us had the same criteria towards all the fans regardless of whether they came from Serbia or if they were local fans, so we did keep the situation totally under control and such incidents were on a minor scale compared to what happened later. These incidents at that time were negligible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. At the beginning we told the Trial Chamber, but I would like you to tell us what ethnic group you belong to.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am an ethnic Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how many years you worked in this town where you actually first got your employment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spent 11 years working in that town, from 1979 to 1990, July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you worked throughout that whole period there, am I right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was employed at the SUP throughout that whole period. That's where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were there any occasions in that period when due to the nature of your job you would go to some other territory or area in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were special situations when you would go to another town or another republic in order to help the police forces in that area. This usually had to do with some major sports events, the Olympic Games, the university sports games, other competitions that I specifically did not go to but my colleagues went. My absences from the town where I worked were mostly related to trips to the region of Kosovo and Metohija in 1982. That's when there were major demonstrations by Albanian demonstrators and irredentists and this mapped mostly in Pristina, Podujevo, and Suva Reka. By a decision of the federal government and the presidency police forces from all republics were engaged and provinces of the then Yugoslavia and they all made up one unit and they all went to the Kosovo and Metohija area in order to maintain public order and prevent demonstrations, destruction, and violent secession, which is what the Albanians at the time were seeking. They were seeking Kosovo to become a republic. In 1981, a number of people went from my town where I was employed. I went in 1982, in April. I was deployed or my unit was deployed in the region of Glogovac, Srbica municipalities near Pristina, in Kosovo. We stayed there for a month and a half. During that time we didn't have any contacts with separatists and everything proceeded without any incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said that you worked for 11 years in the town where you first began to work and you worked at the Secretariat for internal affairs in that town. You also explained that the situation was peaceful and under control and that public order was maintained. Until the end of your employment or stay in that town, did the situation remain unchanged or did anything change?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation as I described it before remained the same until 1990, early 1990, which had to do with the emergence of multi-party activities in Yugoslavia, or rather in Croatia, when the situation changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In 1990, were there any elections held in the Republic of Croatia which was then the Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, if you recall that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990 the first multi-party elections were held in Croatia. They were held in April and early May. The preparations of the elections and the pre-election rallies changed the situation to a large degree in the state in the republic and in the town where I lived, the situation changed for the worse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I request -- I know the interpreters have not complained but I hear that the witness begins to answer while you are still asking your question. If you could try to make sure that you and the witness give pauses in between questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I failed to warn the witness to make these pauses, so thank you for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, because we understand each other and the interpreting service is obliged to interpret my question and your answer, could you please pause between the question and before you begin answering so that we do not overlap and so that everything could be interpreted, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Milovancevic. You also forget.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said that these pre-election rallies in early 1990, before the elections, led to a change in the situation in your town and other places and throughout the Republic of Croatia. Can you tell us briefly what these changes entailed, how was this manifested? How did you find out about these things?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about that because I am -- I participated directly in those events. The events were obvious because all the parties that were founded were for the most part nationalist parties and their rallies were -- had a sort of nationalist tone. All of them propagated being freed or liberated from something. So these parties and primarily I'm talking about the Croatian Democratic Union and there was the federal government in Belgrade, actually the attitude of the HDZ was that the federal government in Belgrade was taking all the money from all the republics, particularly tourist revenues from Croatia and that everyone in the other republics was living on the money from Croatia and they promised that if we got an independent state, no one would be able to live at the expense of Croatian citizens. They always used the word Croats, not citizens. We Serbs and others in these talks were not even mentioned in a good light because when there was such talk, it was always "we Croats," they never addressed the citizens of Croatia, "Croats and others." Such rallies irritated the others, and Croats themselves to a certain extent who were not all in favour of them because they knew what this would lead to because many people still remembered the Second World War, the fratricidal war in which Serbs and Croats waged civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said that these election rallies were a place where it was said that Croatia was being exploited by the rest of Yugoslavia. That's how I understood what you said. Please correct me if I'm wrong. Do you have information if something like this is true or not, if it's correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said is correct, that it was the slogan of these election rally speakers. What I can say is that there is no basis for believing that something like that is true because at that time the Prime Minister or the federal government president was Ante Markovic, a Croat, and before that, former presidents of the federal government for the most part were also Croats. I can just mention Mikelic, Mijlka Plenans [phoen], before that, the late Dzemal Bijedic, who was a Muslim. I don't recall any Serb before that being Prime Minister. I don't recall anything like that, so I think that they, as Prime Ministers and members of the government, there were ministers from various republics, would not permit any kind of inequality, would not allow their country to be robbed and money to go to other places without any need for something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. So in relation to your answer, so what is your opinion, why was this being stated in the election rallies? What was the objective of such speeches?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the objective was to awaken nationalist feelings amongst the voters, amongst the citizens of Croatia, Croats, to secure their votes and also to win power, in order to implement ideas that they had conceived at that time. So the idea was to secure legitimacy, to win power in elections and the easiest way to do that was to touch upon nationalist feelings by saying that Croats for a thousand years waited to get their own state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So in relation to that, can you tell us, if you know, who at that time was at the head of the Yugoslav Republic of Croatia, Croats or someone else, Croatian leadership or a different leadership?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, in reference to that question, I'm not sure right now what time we are talking about. "At that time" if we could have clarification on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank my learned friend. Perhaps I was a little bit imprecise. We are talking about early 1990 and the election campaign prior to the first multi-party elections in April and May 1990. So when I said "at that time," what I meant was early 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was inadvertent and I thank my learned friend from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, can you give us a brief answer, please?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time all the responsible posts in the Republic of Croatia were held for the most part by Croats, and there was a number of Serbs. Vilim Mulc, a Croat, at the time was head of the republican MUP -- the member of the Croatian -- the Croatian member of the federal Presidency was Stipe Suvar. All the main posts were held by Croats. And in these election rallies, they were described as communists and servants of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: These election rallies, was there any talk about the national question in any way?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was discussed in the sense that it was always stressed that there were many policemen, Serbs, in the police forces, and that there will have to be a reorganisation of the police itself in order to balance out these percentages, in order to have the percentages correspond to the population percentages. So the percentages in the police would have to correspond to the actual percentages amongst the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what was the response to such a topic? How was that received? Talk about the number of employees of an ethnic group other than one's own ethnic group, these kind of comparisons? How was this received in the public, in the press, and in communication amongst people, if you can tell us?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After living together in peace for a long time, frequent reference to such topics and the offering of various solutions caused confusion and anxiety among citizens, including members of the police force, not only Serbs who were already beginning to see that something nasty was going to happen, but also Croats, who were mostly pro-Yugoslav and they realised they would have to be apologetic before the new authorities as regards their prior record in the service, and they were already beginning to grumble. New iconography already appeared, new flags, without the five-pointed star and with the Croatian chequerboard instead, which the Croats called the old, ancient, historic coat of arms of the Croats. However, such flags caused anxiety among the Serbs because it was the same as the flag of the Independent State of Croatia from the times of the Second World War when Croatia was an ally of Hitler's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Might I ask a question whilst you're on this area, if you don't mind. Mr. Witness, at the time, you have mentioned the fact that there were many Serb policemen in the police force. Was there at the time or were there more Serb policemen than Croat policemen, or policemen of other ethnic groups? What was the sort of balance, in terms of percentages? I would just like to find out because you've said that there was a lot of concern about that. So I'd like to find out at this stage. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time, I don't know exactly. I don't have data about the whole territory of Croatia but it is certain that there were more Croats, not many more, though. As for the profession of policemen, that particular profession was far from being a privilege at that time, in that system. It was mainly a profession chosen by poor people and their careers depended mainly on their training and personal capabilities. To be a policeman was not a very attractive job. On the contrary, policemen were the subject of jokes and even slurs among the citizenry and we often experienced problems because of our profession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think I did not put my question clear enough. Or I have misunderstood your evidence. I understood you to be saying that there was concern expressed by Croats within the framework of the political system at the time, or certainly the rallies and the parties, to the effect that there were many Serb policemen in the police force. So what I'm trying to discover from you is were there greater numbers of Serb policemen in the force than Croats or policemen of other ethnic groups? And if you could give an idea what -- how it panned out in terms of the numbers of the respective ethnic groups, particularly with reference to the number of Serbs as against, say, Croats. That specifically. And you could keep it short and just say because it could be dealt with fairly easily.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, from what I know, at that time, it is certain that there were more Croats on the police force, but they did not outnumber Serbs by that much. However, yes, there were more Croats than others, Serbs, Muslims, and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So it's the fact that there were so many Serbs in the force in proportion to the number of Serbs in the population as against Serb policemen actually outnumbering Croat policemen, then? From what I understand. Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Milovancevic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Within the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia at the time, I am picking up on the question asked of you by Honourable Judge Nosworthy, there were policemen belonging to various ethnic groups; is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: A relatively high percentage of policemen of Serb ethnicity, you would explain in which way? I just want us to come back to this issue once again.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This high percentage of Serb policemen in the MUP of Croatia is explained by the fact that as I said, the profession of policeman was not an attractive one at the time in the Republic of Croatia because it didn't bring any benefits or privileges, any high earnings. On the contrary, it was a profession of poor people who had family or other background in uniformed professions. Also, it was historically an area of Krajina's border military areas where the population was mostly poor people who traditionally went to work in the army, whereas Croats were oriented towards the coast and tourism where they could get in one month the annual salary of a policeman. But I can tell you that most of the senior personnel on the police force were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: For instance, if one found a job in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, wherever he was stationed, he or she were stationed, were there any requirements to be fulfilled?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there were certain requirements that every candidate had to meet in order to be admitted into the ministry or, rather, the republican Secretariat of the Interior of Croatia, as it was called. There were two ways in which one could become an employee of the Ministry of the Interior, either through regular training, that is four years of secondary schooling in Zagreb, in a specialised high school, and also higher schools such as the two year higher school in Zagreb, or by getting extra training, which means after the secondary school and after doing one's military service, there was a training centre with a one-year course in Fazane, near Pula. That was another way because the graduates of that school would become policemen. In addition to that, there were a few other are requirements for a prospective employee. One was called moral and political suitability, meaning that a candidate did not come from a family bent on subversive activities in the past, that nobody served in enemy formations in the past war, that the person and nobody in their family was a member of the quisling, Ustasha units, et cetera. The candidate had to be physically fit and in good health, and that they had no record of a social behaviour or mental illness. There was vetting conducted in one's place of residence and employment to check that the person had no criminal record, no prior convictions, no record of misdemeanours, violations of public law and order, asocial behaviour, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You gave us a very extensive answer on the subject, but my question was directed at something specific. Citizenship, did the candidate have to have a particular citizenship and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in the Republic of Croatia, anybody was allowed to apply as long as they had the citizenship of the SFRY, SFR Yugoslavia, that is. A candidate could come from Macedonia or any other republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, that last statement does explain my question. I was going to ask, could anybody come from anywhere in Yugoslavia. You didn't have to be from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just another brief question that I omitted to ask you before. Who decided on applications to the Ministry of the Interior, applications for employment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That decision was made by a commission set up at the headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was it then the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Decisions on employment were made in Zagreb and employment contracts were made in Zagreb, whereupon successful applicants were assigned all over the republic, but not to their hometown. It was a rule that nobody was assigned to their hometown. Of course, there were certain exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. We are talking about year 1990 still, about election rallies. Can you tell us, what was the outcome of the first multi-party elections in 1990, if you know, and did it reflect in any way on the work of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The outcome of the first multi-party elections in Croatia in 1990 was the victory of the Croatian Democratic Union, HDZ, and its coming into power had a negative impact on the state, on the republic. I will explain. At that time, the party had not yet started specific activities to take over power, but the citizenry was already unsettled. There was discontent among the people because they were afraid for their future, and afraid because of all the things they had seen at election rallies, and I have forgotten to mention before that in March 1990, there was a major incident in a place called Benkovac in Dalmatia. It was a rally of the Croatian Democratic Union, and the then president of the party, who later became president of the republic, held a speech during which there was an attempt to attack him as he was speaking at the rostrum, and this resulted in a conflict between the Croats and the Serbs who were standing by and following this rally, and there ensued a general brawl. I watched that on television the next day. The MUP of Croatia issued a report saying that ballistic experts confirmed that the plastic pistol with which a Serb had attempted to kill Mr. Tudjman could not have fired any real bullets. However, this caused major disorder in Benkovac and supporters of the HDZ used this incident to claim at future rallies that Serbs were jeopardising the democratic future of Croatia and trying to prevent free speech, and that was repeated later when three MPs of Croat ethnicity were killed. Such claims were always greeted with ovation and applause, and this was used to inflame the masses. I remember another rally that was held in Split on the coast, because I was in that town at the time, and there were columns of vehicles returning from that rally, and as they passed by the police station, they honked, made various provocations and waved the flags that had not yet been allowed at that time, and that was a violation of the regulations, and they also put stickers on surrounding vehicles, stickers with the chequerboard sign. And all this caused great anxiety among a certain group of the population that feared a repetition of all the things that had already lapped to them between 1941 and 1945.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see in the translation that there is an abbreviation, there is a reference to three MPs of Croat ethnicity. What does MP mean in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Member of parliament, deputy to the Croat assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, interpreter. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. Just wanted to be sure. I suspected that was the case.

utterances.speaker: THE FRENCH INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter from the French booth would like to say it's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... an assassination attempt against Mr. Tudjman --

utterances.speaker: THE FRENCH INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Kingdom of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... something that happened in 1929, so could you just very briefly so that we don't waste too much time, can you please tell us what happened in 1929 so that there is no confusion there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, first of all, I think there was an attempt at an intervention from the French booth. They were trying to tell us something, but secondly, as a result of that, I missed the first part of that question and from what I could catch it sounded awfully leading but I can't be terribly sure but I missed the question. I wonder if we could find out what it was that was coming from the French booth and then maybe he could ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you proceed, Mr. Milovancevic, I also heard something from the French booth. Could the French booth please say what it wanted to say? The interpreters need the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French booth said that it was on the transcript Croatian assembly. It's not Croatian assembly in 1929 because it was the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. The three MPs who have been killed haven't been killed in the Croatian assembly but in the assembly of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Interpreter, but unfortunately we've got to go by what the witness says and -- but we are grateful for what you have just said. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, wait a minute. Did this witness say anything about 1929?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. He mentioned 1929 and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and I think that that part is not in the transcript, but perhaps we can deal with that after the break so what I have told you now I'm going to use to reformulate the question to the witness and I think then there will be also it will shall much clearer to my learned friend Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you want to reformulate it now or do you want to reformulate it after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we can do that after the break, Your Honour, because it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just remind you, Mr. Milovancevic, we are in open session, just to remind you that we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, in the transcript, I think it was a little bit unclear what you said, the translation was a little bit unclear. So could you please tell us again what happened with this killing of three Members of Parliament? You mentioned that event. I don't want to mention anything, the year. When you were talking about the events in the assembly of Yugoslavia and the possible assassination against Mr. Tudjman, do you remember that part?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I wanted to mention that -- I'm not a historian but I know that this happened in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenians in 1928 or 1929 in the parliament of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, a member of parliament of Serb ethnicity, after he was insulted by a Croatian member of parliament, took out his pistol and shot at Croat deputies and he killed two or three Members of Parliament of Croat ethnicity. That event happened then. After these incidents in Benkovac in 1990, the leadership of the HDZ used that to compare these two incidents, saying that back then, they were victims of Serbs and in that way presenting themselves as victims now, they were gaining points and favour amongst their own voters. This is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem. I hear more the witness than the interpreter on my headphone, and the witness comes much louder than the interpreter. I can't even hear what the interpreter is saying. I don't know whether it's just my headphone or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I have a question about these two incidents which you're saying happened. Which two incidents do you mean? The one is what you talked about in 1928 or 1929, and the other one, please, was which? Which one? The other one was the -- in modern times, you mean? The toy pistol or plastic pistol being used against President Tudjman? Can you clarify that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second incident occurred in 1990, in March, during the election rallies. This is the second incident, with the plastic pistol. This was in 1990. But at subsequent rallies, they linked this incident with the other one, making it seem as if the intention was to destroy the Croatian leadership and in that way, presenting themselves as victims, they gained more popularity and more points amongst their own voters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. Thank you very much for the indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, who was the Minister of Internal Affairs of Croatia up until the multi-party elections that took place in April and May 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The republican SUP minister before the elections was Vilim Mulc.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: After the HDZ victory in these first multi-party elections in 1990, who became the Minister of the Croatian SUP?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new first SUP minister in the Croatian government after the multi-party election was a Croat, Josip Boljkovac. He's the one who replaced Vilim Mulc.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to put a few questions now that could possibly identify the witness. These questions relate to his activities or movements within the service. So I would like to request that we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the time when you assumed your new post, can you please tell us what the structure of the Knin public security station was? How many employees, how many staff did it have?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the Knin public security station had between 95 and 100 staff. This is the total number of staff. Of that, 70 of them were police officers, inspectors, and others, while the rest, about 30 of them, was technical staff, administrative staff, and the support services.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, can you tell us what the situation was in terms of the work atmosphere at the police station, the interpersonal relations?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already at the time when I arrived in mid-July, there were already, how shall I put it, certain tensions and a certain turmoil at the station, and that was because already in early July 1990, 54 or 55 staff members of the Knin SUP had signed a petition addressed to the republican MUP, the federal Ministry of the Interior and some other institutions, stating that they would not accept to wear the chequerboard emblem on their caps and that they would not be called by the new Croatian term for policemen, redarstvenik, and that they would not accept the new Croatian term for the police station, which was postojna, all because these terms associated in their minds with the terminology of the NDH, the Independent State of Croatia of the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What was the ethnic structure of the public security station in Knin at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the total of 100 or so employees, around 10, including policemen, inspectors and support staff, were Croats, and I think there were two Muslims. The rest were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you tell us who were the signatories of that petition that you just mentioned, in terms of their ethnicity, I mean, if you know?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe all the signatories of that petition were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say Serbs, you mean policemen, employees of the public security station in Knin?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean policemen and other employees of the station. I don't mean citizens at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did all the employees sign the petition? Did all Serb employees sign?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He said 54 or 55 staff members of the Knin SUP had signed the petition so it couldn't be all. Did you hear that, Mr. Milovancevic? If you look at page 36, line 14, the witness said 54 or 55 staff members of the Knin SUP had signed the petition. So it cannot be all of them. The majority of them definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is clear, Your Honour. Let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did that petition have any impact on the atmosphere and the situation at the police station and did any proceedings take place?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not everybody signed the petition, and I should add something that is important to this case. There was a leaflet, a flyer circulating around the town naming eight Serb employees of that police station who had not signed the petition. So in addition to the signatories, who were 54 or 55, there were eight who did not sign and those eight were officers. I don't know if there were more Serbs in the station but if you add the 55 who signed and eight who did not, I don't know if that gives us a total of all the Serbs who were employed. I don't know because I wasn't there, and I didn't particularly pay attention to that later. So I cannot tell you the total number of Serb employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the public security station in Knin at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, the commander of the police station was Ivan Brzoja, a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: After you took up your new post at this police station, did you proceed to establish contact with higher authorities and agencies within the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in daily contact with them by telephone, telex, and we sent reports daily to the higher command in Sibenik covering all activities that had taken place on our territory in the past 24 hours. In addition to that, at least once a week, I would go to attend meetings in Sibenik where senior staff meetings of the Sibenik SUP took place, and I belonged to that SUP organisationally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was such conduct on your part in keeping with the regular practice or did it divert from that practice in any way?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the prevailing practice that had become customary over the years, and it was typical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the time when you assumed your new post in Knin, in mid-July 1990, the elections were over. Who was in charge of the municipal authorities in Knin at the time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serbian Democratic Party that had won the elections in Knin, and at that time Milan Babic was president of the municipality and the president of the executive council was Veljko Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you transferred from your prior workplace to Knin, did you have a meeting with Mr. Babic? Did you meet him? Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is customary for representatives of the municipal authorities and members of the public security station to cooperate. Their jobs require it. And they monitored each other's activities. Of course, everybody worked within their field of expertise but there were some points of contact between our respective lines of work and we would meet occasionally to sum up the situation and make proposals. However, my meeting with Mr. Babic and Mr. Veljko Popovic did not take place immediately but 10 or 12 days after I first arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can recall it now, it was the usual, the security situation in the territory of the municipality, and since it was summertime, traffic jams were usual for that season in that town, and we must have discussed how to improve the traffic situation, and to keep the station working regularly in its domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What you just told us, does that fit within the regular scheme of communication between the public security station and the municipal authorities?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that is part of the regular and normal communication between those two agencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding that petition that you mentioned a moment ago, what was your attitude to your staff? Did you know any of them from before, and what approach did you take when you came?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, I will say something to you before we proceed. I don't know whether you're aware of this. When the transcript is redacted, we are only trying to prevent your being identified, but the text is still in the transcript. So please don't worry about this. Everything you say is part of your testimony before the Tribunal. Do you understand? Thank you. May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Save to explain that what happens when a redaction takes place is that what -- that part is not published to the outside world. That's the only difference. Am I right? You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, what was your attitude toward those policemen who signed the petition and those who didn't?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that my attitude toward those who signed the petition was identical as my attitude to those who didn't sign it. This means that they continued to do the tasks and assignments that were intended for them and for the positions they were filling. I made no distinction between them. Nor did I observe any of them asking for privileges, nor would I have granted any privileges to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you were giving them their work assignments, did you treat them all the same, those who signed and those who didn't sign the petition?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty roster and the work schedule for the policemen working on the beat was drawn up by the police station commander or his deputy, whereas the work schedule of inspectors and detectives was done by their immediate superior, the superior of the crime department. I never drew up such rosters myself, except if there was an important task in hand, as an exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, can you give us an example of such an exception, such an important task?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that I recall two instances from that time period. In one instance, policemen had -- and inspectors had to be assigned to go and secure the rally in Srb on the 25th of July 1990. I myself drew up the list of those who were assigned to go and assist the Donji Lapac and Gracac police force in securing that rally. Another instance, the second one, was when the police had to help carry out a task when construction workers in the road construction company, Sibenik, had to remove some road signs, the Knin board, and I sent a team consisting of four policemen who had signed the petition and four who hadn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Before I ask you about these particular events, can you tell us what your impression is as to how the staff of Knin police station carried out their duties, with respect to the existing legislation and rules and regulations on the work of the police station?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evaluating the way they carried out their assignments, I can say that they did so very well. They were very successful in maintaining public law and order, and in detecting and solving crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You mentioned securing the rally in Srb. Can you tell us when this happened and how many policemen were sent to assist in securing the rally?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rally in Srb was held, as far as I can recall, on the 25th of July 1990. On that occasion, the chiefs of the police station in Donji Lapac, to which Srb belonged, assessed the rally as a high-risk event because of the number of participants and because of the prevailing situation in the area at the time. The rally was evaluated as a high-risk event and because there were to be very many participants and the police station had few policemen, they asked for reinforcements from neighbouring public security stations. I received an order therefore to participate with a certain number of men, I think 10 to 15 authorised police officers, and to send them from the Knin public security station to Srb to help secure the rally. This was all done within the Sibenik SUP organisation. I provided some 15 employees who participated in preparing the securing of the rally. This means the following. I designated those 15 policemen and inspectors, and in the early morning, a bus arrived in front of the police station with policemen from Sibenik and Drnis who were also on their way to help secure the rally. The officers from Knin got on to the bus and left to carry out their task. Later on, I heard that they hadn't been deployed in Srb itself but that they were in Gracac police station on standby.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You have given a very detailed description of the way this assignment was carried out. Can you tell us briefly what the task of the police at that rally was? Why did the police go there to secure the rally? What did that involve?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police always went to rallies in order to maintain public law and order and to prevent any disorder organised by individuals or happening spontaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. At this rally in Srb, were there any incidents? Did the police intervene?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the police did not need to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you arrived in the Knin public security station, was Mr. Martic employed there?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Martic was employed in that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what was his post?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was an operative in crime prevention. He was an inspector, a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic participate in the rally in Srb?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he didn't, because he was designated to help secure the rally, by me. The entire group, not just he, was on standby in the Gracac public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll just put one more question about the rally in Srb. Do you know what the topic of the rally in Srb was, what it was about?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never involved in politics, either then or now, but as far as I can recall, a declaration on the sovereignty of the Serb people in Croatia was adopted and the Serb National Council was elected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you mentioned the situation where you sent a mixed team, so to say, a team consisting of those who signed the petition and those who didn't. It concerned the removal of some sign-posts. Can you describe in greater detail what kind of sign-posts were being removed, who ordered their removal, and how this intervention ended?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each town or settlement had sign-posts at its entrance bearing the name of the place, informing the travellers what town or place they were entering. So at Knin at four exits and entrances to the town there were sign-posts with the name Knin. They were in the Cyrillic script. In the Socialist Republic of Croatia, Croatia at the time, the law on script and language was still in force in which Cyrillic was equal to the Latin script. So the sign-posts were in the Cyrillic script. The day before, the secretary of the Sibenik SUP, Ante Bujas called me and informed me that Marko Slavica would come to see me. He was the director of the road maintenance company of Sibenik, who were also responsible for the roads in the Knin sector, that he wanted to discuss something with me, and that I should offer him help if he needed in order for him to carry out the assignment that he was going to be carrying out. The next day, this gentleman, Mr. Slavica came to my office, I knew him from before, and he told me that as the director of the road maintenance company was given an order from Zagreb -- I think it was the transport ministry -- that he received an order from them to remove the sign-posts for Knin in the Cyrillic language that were placed at these four entrances and exits to the town, and that other than his workers who were going to remove these sign-posts, he needed police presence who would protect the workers in the event that they were attacked or anything like that. We agreed then that the next day at 8.00 we would carry out this action, his workers should come to the police station with foremen and that I would provide an adequate number of officers, police officers, so that they could then proceed to carry out their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me whether you fulfilled this agreement? Did these SUP workers go with these other workers who were supposed it remove these sign-posts, and if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, I allocated eight policemen from the Knin public security station to help in the implementation of that task. I deliberately assigned four workers who signed this petition and four workers who did not sign this petition for this particular job. I did this deliberately so that nobody could say that I was protecting a particular group, those who signed or those who did not sign. So I allocated that there should be pairs going on the assignment, one person who had signed and the other one who had not signed. My staff didn't even know what assignment it was until I told them in the morning, together with the workers of this road maintenance company. I told them what the assignment was and that their task was only to protect the other workers from the road maintenance company to prevent them from getting injured or hurt in there should be any attacks when the sign-posts were being removed. Soon, one patrol and then another patrol informed me that in places where they had arrived, the workers had started to take down the sign-posts, to dig them up, and that a large number of citizens had begun to gather, that they objected to what the workers were doing, they were insulting them, threatening them, so they sought my instructions. I didn't want to make this decision alone so I consulted with secretary Bujas. I told him what the problem was. I told him what it could further cause and he told me to stop the implementation of this task. At one of the places where the task was being carried out, a TV crew appeared and they filmed the entire event. I think that it was a TV crew from Belgrade television. They were making some sort of programme in Knin at the time. They also wanted interview with me but I refused that because I was not authorised to give interviews without prior consent of my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear of a decision to organise a referendum in August 1990?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard of a decision to have a referendum or to conduct a referendum, and I was actually at the time living in that area, so that I know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The referendum was scheduled for late August 1990. Were there any problems in relation to that, that had to do with the work of the public security station in Knin?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually we very briefly discussed the referendum at a very short meeting with my colleagues in Sibenik, when it was stated that the police in Knin should not get involved too much, in view of the fact that the situation was very complicated, that it should not undertake actions or measures in relation to the referendum, but the bodies in other municipalities were told that if they should find some voting leaflets or something, should then question the person where they found this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you have problems in your work that had anything to do with the referendum?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the referendum itself, nothing of that reflected on our work, the referendum itself. But shortly before the referendum was held, a few days before, the security situation in Knin deteriorated, in Knin and its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In what sense did the situation deteriorate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what happened was that on the 17th of August 1990, weapons were seized from the Knin public security station belonging to the reserve police forces of the Knin station. So that incident, as a consequence, led to changes in the security situation and reflected on the referendum itself and on the general situation in Knin and in a number of other municipalities. You could even say that it had an effect on the situation in the republic and the state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, when you say that the weapons were seized from the Knin public security station, could you please tell us what these weapons were?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public security station in Knin, just like all the other stations, municipal stations, on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, as well as on the territory of Yugoslavia, were actually weapons of the police reserve forces. These were long-barrelled weapons, guns, I mean rifles, pistols, fewer pistols, and they were there in case of immediate threat of war or immediate danger. The reserve police would be called in and these weapons would be issued to them so that they would be able to carry out their tasks. Besides these weapons, the station also had trophy hunting weapons which were confiscated from citizens by police officers if there were some violations involving those hunting weapons. These weapons were kept at the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Talking about the reserve forces' weapons, was that ever a topic of conversation between you and your superiors?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time these weapons were discussed was on the 16th of August 1990. In the evening, approximately at 9.00 or 10.00 p.m. in the village of Velim near Stankovci in the house of a colleague of mine, Zoran Perica, who at the time was the chief of the Drnis police station --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that now would be a good time to go on our break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break, come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Before the break, sir, you mentioned weapons of the reserve forces of the police at the public security station in Knin. Can you please tell us who called you to that meeting, where was it held, and who attended it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was summoned to the meeting by the SUP secretary, Ante Bujas. He happened to be in Zagreb and he scheduled the meeting at about 9.00 p.m. or 10.00 p.m. in the Velim village near Stankovci, in Velim in the house of the Drnis public security station chief, the meeting was attended by the secretary and the chief of the Sibenik SUP and that is where we met and that is where we held the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the date that the meeting was held in you mentioned it before the break. I think you said that it was in the evening and you mentioned the date.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 16th of August, the 16th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1990. We are talking about 1990 throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. What was agreed at that meeting, if anything was agreed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretary spoke very briefly and he said the decision had been made that weapons from the reserve force in Knin and Sibenik public security stations would be withdrawn because the new recruits needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's what the head of SUP Sibenik told you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the secretary of the Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did he tell you how and when to do this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening, we made a plan how to carry this out. We agreed that we would do it with the assistance of several of the employees who had not signed that petition back then, and that it should be done that night, namely weapons from the depot would be taken and loaded on to a vehicle and then one patrol from Sibenik would arrive and pose as traffic police. In fact, they would be there to secure that shipment of weapons if anyone tried to intercept the vehicle on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you tell us why it was ordered to do this by night? Was it explained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was said that it's necessary to do that by night so that people wouldn't know about it because if people in Knin found out, they would certainly gather and prevent it, and that is because when the petitions of -- when the petition was signed by that staff in Knin, and when the senior officers from Sibenik came to discuss this petition and see what happened in that case, even then a large number of citizens gathered around the police station and there was some kind of protest meeting. So anticipating that again there could be a rally, a protest rally, it was decided to do that by night. Drnis was a municipality in which the population was mixed, half/half. It was decided that it could maybe be done in the morning on the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you act upon this order of your seniors? Did you proceed with that assignment to withdraw the weapons from the depot?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried. I went to Sibenik with my colleague, Mr. Perica, to make -- to discuss the details of the plan, to discuss code words, communications, the patrol that would come to secure the shipment, et cetera. So I set out to Knin. And on my way, I informed one of the staff members of the Knin police station who hadn't signed the petition that he should wait for me at the petrol station at a certain designated time, I think it was 1.00 a.m., about one kilometre from Knin, and at that designated time we met up at the petrol station and I told him what had been agreed and what our assignment was, and if we needed more people to help us, we should go and inform them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of that staff member of the Knin public security station, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. He was an inspector, Rajko Junar [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You said you met up around 1.00 a.m. at the petrol station in Knin, and did you indeed go to the police station to withdraw the weapons?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't because while presenting the assignment and discussing the details, this officer got scared, he placed his hands on his head, he said, "There is no way we can carry it out."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got into my car, my civilian car, passenger car. We passed by the police station and there was a low wall outside, and there were a couple of citizens, in fact quite a few citizens outside, and there were many in the streets. So it was our assessment that it was impossible to perform that mission without anybody noticing. We would certainly be found out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So did you give up? Was it your own decision to give up?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to a business company, I called the secretary, Bujas, from their telephone, and described to him the situation as it was, and I told him it was impossible to perform the assignment and he told me to wait, to hold, and when he picked up again he told me he had consulted with the senior officers in Zagreb and that their decision was to give up the whole mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you go home after that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't because at that time, I didn't have an apartment in Knin. I would spend the nights at various friends. My own home was 50 kilometres away from Knin. I went to my office and got to sleep there. I decided to wait for dawn there because it made no sense to go home and then back. So I spent the night at the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It was already after midnight, it was already the 17th of August 1990. Since that date is very well known in our parts, can you tell us what happened around the public security station?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime after 2.00 a.m. - I hadn't managed to go to sleep yet - I heard a lot of noise and commotion around the police station. I went down to the ground floor where the duty officer's office was. There were several officers and some citizens there. In fact, it was quite a crowd. And I was informed that weapons were removed from the police station in Obrovac and a similar attempt was made in Benkovac, also at the public security station. A lot of people had gathered and the attempt to remove the weapons was abolished, was renounced. But the citizens already had a hunch that a similar attempt would be made in Knin and there was a lot of speculation going on. They asked me who was going to come, who had the authorisation, I told hem -- I tried to call them down, I told them that nothing would happen. I did not reveal to them that I was in fact entrusted with removing the weapons, that it was my assignment. I told them to go home and to calm down. Since the situation was very tense and there was a lot of work to do, and I had no appropriate dwelling in Knin, I went back to the office and nothing more happened until the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did something happen the next morning?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, on the 17th of August, in the morning hours, clusters of people gathered all about town, they discussed the removal of weapons in Obrovac, in Benkovac, and they were wondering how come nothing happened in Knin, and everybody commented and interpreted it as attempts to disarm the people like it was done back in 1941 when weapons were seized from all Serbs to prevent possible insurgencies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request could counsel turn off the microphone because we hear the shuffling of papers more than anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So the next morning, around 10.00 you went to Sibenik. You mean SUP Sibenik. Did you go there, was it your own decision to go there or was it your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, where did he say he was going to Sibenik the following morning? You asked him, did something happen the next morning, and then he says, the next on the 17th of August in the morning lots of people gathered all over our town, they discussed the removal of weapons in Obrovac and Benkovac and they were wondering how come nothing happened in Knin. And everybody commented and interpreted it as an attempt to disarm the people like it was done back in 1941 when weapons were seized from all Serbs to prevent possible insurgencies. He doesn't even say anything about Sibenik. I know that the interpreter intervened at that stage but on the record, there is nothing about Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not turn off my microphone and probably that paper that was shuffling was my paper and I'll take better care of it in the future. I just asked the witness a question that did relate to his prior answer. Let me just ask him now if he had mentioned Sibenik in relation to that morning of the 17th of August 1990.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 17th of August 1990, sometime around 10 or maybe 11.00, I went to Sibenik, and when I speak about these towns, I always mean the police institutions there. So I didn't think it was necessary to always specify that it was SUP Sibenik that I went to. I did go there and I was indeed invited by my superiors, probably to explain why the mission wasn't carried out, why it failed, and I had some car trouble on the road. My car stopped and wouldn't budge any more. So somehow I managed to reach the police station in Drnis, from where I called Sibenik. Or maybe -- yes, yes, now I remember. Somebody from Sibenik came to Drnis, the assistant chief, and we discussed the event and he then suggested a new plan, namely that they would send from SUP Sibenik to the police security station in Knin some car mechanics, two or three of them, but only one of them would actually know what needed to be done, and his task and mine was to get a police van, normally used for transportation of prisoners, and bring it to the garage purportedly for repairs. From that garage there was a subterranean corridor leading to the arms depot. And that car mechanic was supposed to break the door with me, go in with me, remove the weapons, load them into that special police van, and under the pretext that he was going to try out the car after repair, he was going to take it to Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
