utterances.text: Witness, you were an employee there. You had a job in the police station in Knin. Now, another policeman sent from the Sibenik SUP was coming to your turf, so to speak. Why would you have to break the door to the arms depot?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said before, when we had that plan to do it by night, we were aware all the time that the removal of weapons would be very badly received in town and in the whole municipality. It would lead the people to gather in a protest rally, and God knows what that could turn into. Therefore, instructions were given to do it in secret and the consequences that might ensue did not in my opinion interest anyone very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honours, did I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was going to ask if I could interrupt. But you had -- now you've asked the question. You go ahead with your question. Okay. Maybe for us to understand this whole discussion, are you able to tell us why it was decided that you must remove these weapons? Why were these weapons supposed to be removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I tried to explain before, at that meeting in Velim on the 16th of August, I was informed that those weapons were needed to arm new members of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, that new personnel was admitted into the service but had no weapons and they had to be given weapons that normally were stored for the reserve force in various depots of various police stations. Such weapons were in storage also, among other places, in the public security station in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where was this new personnel supposed to be receiving these weapons from you? Where were they stationed, these new personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that meeting held on the 16th of August, we were not told where these new personnel members were, and I was not told in what other places in Croatia weapons were to be taken from police stations. I didn't know that they were be taken from Obrovac, Benkovac and Knin, but one can conclude from everything that weapons were taken from towns with a majority-Serb population. As for the new employees for whom the weapons were intended, what I can say is that the first time I heard about new employees in the police station was in August 1990 at a senior staff meeting in the Sibenik SUP, to which I belonged, when a new senior staff member turned up from Zagreb, his name was Generalija I had never heard of him before, and during this meeting, he said that he had brought a group of newly recruited policemen to Sibenik. He said that they had been accommodated in the Sibenik old people's home, that they were unemployed or rather they were not given anything to do and that they were causing disorder, that they were fighting, gambling, and he asked the senior staff members for assistance in doing something about this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that answer is fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: If I might -- now that Judge Moloto has asked questions on this area I had a couple of questions myself marked down. Mr. Witness, where would new recruits normally have got weapons from? From which source would weapons normally come from for new recruits? That's one of the things I want to know from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I entered employment in the Split SUP, I was issued with a short-barrel, a pistol, and a long barrel, a rifle, in the Split police station. Each police station had its own small depot where weapons were kept and which were issued to their employees. The rule was that inspectors always carried pistols with them. They could either take them home or leave them in their lockers in the police station. Rifles could not be taken out of the police station. They always had to be kept in the police station, and they could be taken out only during annual target practice, for cleaning, or with special permission when going on a high-risk assignment where such weapons might be used. Each police station had its depot and issued weapons to its employees. The largest MUP depot was in Zagreb, in the headquarters where there were large quantities of weapons used to arm new recruits. I do not know whether many more employees were recruited at one time more than were weapons available to arm them. This was a month in which a new generation of policemen graduating from school had already been admitted into the police force armed and sent off to their duties. The conclusion one can reach is that the Ministry of the Interior was withdrawing weapons from those police stations where there was a majority Serb population. I have to repeat that this is a conclusion I drew. I never saw any documents officially issued to this effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is there any particular reason why you believe this other than the historic reason that you've given us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I couldn't say I had any evidence to support this, especially not written evidence but I consider that there was no need to employ these new recruits. The security situation had not deteriorated in the republic to an extent that would require the employment of new policemen. Some policemen were pensioned off so that new job vacancies came into existence but in my view, this was not quite logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Continue, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your last reply concerned the van coming to the Knin security station. Do you remember this, witness?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Excuse me. You explained that you and another man designated by the Sibenik SUP arrived in order to remove these weapons secretly, covertly, so as not to cause a public outcry. Did you finish this task? Did you complete it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not, because, once again, when the mechanics arrived in the workshop and started fixing the vehicle, there were a few policemen passing by and some citizens passing through the courtyard. This man, the mechanic, given the task of removing those weapons, together with me, became frightened and he said he couldn't do it. He asked me to telephone Secretariat Bujas and I let him do that. We again went to a company, because I didn't want to make the phone call from the public security station since I wasn't certain of all these lines and whether someone could hear or not, so we went to a company, called, the secretary explained the situation to him, and then again he agreed to abandon the task and to have the mechanics return to the base in Sibenik without having completed their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did this actually happen as it was agreed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what happened next on the 17th of August? You say it was around 1200 hours. After the mechanics left without having done that job, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. In front of the station, groups of people began to gather. They were commenting on the removal of weapons, saying that special police units were on their way to Knin to remove weapons from Knin, as the weapons hadn't been removed. People started to assemble and at one point the alarm was sounded in town. The siren began to sound. People were arriving in front of the police station from all directions. Suddenly, there were several thousand people gathered in front of the police station. They were shouting, they entered the police station. I informed Sibenik from my office about what was happening. I said the situation was deteriorating. I reported all the facts. They called the Zagreb MUP, the headquarters. Several members of the police who were former chiefs and who lived in Knin arrived in my office. They had previously been chiefs of police and they spoke to the people in Zagreb and Sibenik on the phone because they knew them better. I had only arrived in Knin about a month before and I didn't know many people. So the former chiefs who were not retired were in a better position to provide details about the situation. The situation became so serious people were yelling that they wanted the police to give them weapons so that they could go and meet the MUP forces who were about to attack the police station and set up a new order. That's what people were saying. Well, of course I refused to give them weapons. I wasn't authorised to issue weapons to the people, and there was no need to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What happened to the weapons on that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around 1500 hours, people entered the station, a large crowd of citizens. There were some six to eight policemen in the station. The others were either off duty or on the ground carrying out assignments. There were never more than that number of policemen in the station itself because it was never necessary. So the station was crowded with citizens. They went downstairs, they broke down the door of the room where the weapons were kept, they carried the weapons out into a small orange van. The make was TAM, so it was locally referred to as a Tamic and they drove off these weapons. I watched this from my window. The situation was very chaotic. Nobody obeyed any orders. I did not know the people who were doing this. I didn't know the civilians who were taking these weapons away. My phones kept ringing. People from Zagreb and from Sibenik asking for information and asking me what I could do to stop this happening, and I said, "Well, there was nothing I could do." I didn't have enough men. The situation was a completely new one. It was unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, you said that there were some seven or eight police employees besides you in the station. Were you armed? Did you have the weapons that belonged to you according to the establishment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course we had our short barrels, our pistols, but nobody issued an order to shoot at the people, nor would I have ordered my men to shoot citizens for breaking into the police station because I felt the situation could be resolved subsequently, that the weapons could later be found if there was political will to do so, that this could be resolved politically, not through bloodshed, which would then be something that could not be repaired or made good afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you say a crowd of people broke into the police station, took away the weapons, and what happened next in Knin? Please just give us the main points.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were carrying rifles and carbines around town, even trophy weapons from World War II, ancient rifles. People were rushing around carrying these weapons. There was a general chaos. Everybody was talking about some kind of attack, about helicopters on their way to Knin to put down the situation. At around 5.00 p.m. Radio Knin broadcast the news and the news reader said that weapons had been confiscated or taken from the police station, that unknown perpetrators had taken weapons, that people were self-organising. Milan Babic, the president of the municipality, as the news reader said, had declared a state of war in the municipality. This was a situation that was completely new to us. None of us policemen had ever experienced anything like this, nor had we been trained how to behave in such a situation. I couldn't ask for instructions from Zagreb any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In this general situation of chaos, was there any shooting?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was some shooting into the air. Nobody knew who was shooting at whom but no one was injured. People were shooting into the air. Rumours spread that special purpose MUP policemen were on their way to Knin with APCs and that at Cupkovica Most, Cupkovica bridge, they had clashed with the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As we have no idea where this place is, can you tell us how far it is from Knin and what your reaction was to this information?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my estimation, as I'm not very familiar with that municipality, I didn't work in it long, I think it's about 15 kilometres away from Knin along the railway tracks. There is a local road running parallel with the railway tracks. The place is called Cupkovica most. When I heard this information, I got into a car with Nikola Rastovic, a police inspector, and my intention was to go there and see what was happening. I felt that this was my duty because I didn't have sufficient number of men to send out patrols to keep me informed. I didn't have the patience to wait for that to be organised, I decided to go out on to the ground myself and to see if there was anything I could do to help. The two of us set out together. In town we found a man whom he knew from before, who also wanted to go there. So we asked him to join us and the three of us set out in that direction and wherever we passed through, people were at the entrances to their villages erecting barricades, using old tires, using tractors, so that we had to zig-zag through these roadblocks. We would stop and ask what was going on and they would say well the MUP special purpose policemen are coming to disarm Knin, to disarm our police. They were very mistrustful towards me because they didn't know me well and they had heard the rumours from before so they pointed their weapons at me and then my colleague, the inspector, would get out of the car to explain and we planned to get through several such check-points, manned by local villagers. We arrived at Cupkovica most and there we found a small group of people were hunting weapons. In a conversation with them, I tried to find out what was happening, where these MUP policemen were, where the wounded were and they said they hadn't seen anyone but they had fired shots into the air because they had heard that MUP policemen were arriving and in order to frighten them and prevent them from going any further, they had fired shots in the air to deter their arrival. I then decided that there was, in fact, no incident, that these were all just rumours, that this had all been made up. So I used my radio to inform Knin, Zagreb, and Sibenik that there was no incident, that there were no injured, no one had been killed, there were just armed people standing guard. And then I went back to Knin and got to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned these barriers on the road and the civilians, citizens that put them up and you mentioned the weapons. How many citizens were there and what was the -- what were the weapons? Let's clarify that, Witness.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Passing through those settlements and through those barricades, I saw groups of some ten people, somewhere there were more, somewhere there were fewer, but mostly it was about ten adult men in the groups. Going through the village I didn't really see children. I didn't -- I think that had I gone -- I think I was going through some kind of regular hours when it would have been normal to meet women, children, others, but it wasn't like that. It was changed. There were mostly men with weapons, mostly they had hunting rifles, maybe there was the odd pistol or so. But I didn't see any modern weapon such as automatic weapons or anything like that. It was mostly old weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You say that you passed through a number of these obstacles on the road and you mentioned that you stopped also. Did you talk to those people and what was your impression based on those conversations? Were those people, upset? How did they seem to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, that question would have been fine if it had stopped with the first question but then the subsequent questions made it into a long leading question. Basically it gave him the answer to the question there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw the question, Your Honour, in order to avoid any misunderstanding. The Prosecutor is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ask the next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: During those few days you were in Knin, that's what I understood from your answers, is that true, witness?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you travelled through that region, you went, moved around Knin and to maces around Knin. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did. I travelled through the municipality and I moved around in the town. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Before this day that you are describing, were there any obstacles or barriers erected?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These barriers were not there before. Nobody encountered anything like that before. With this event, the barriers cropped up, they appeared, they knocked down timber and used that to erect the barriers as the days went by the barriers became bulkier and there were more people each day appearing at those barricades, both in the night and during the day. It was non-stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That first day when you were moving towards Cupkovica bridge where you said that there was shooting and where they pointed weapons at you, those people that were at the barriers, what was their mood like?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The weapons were pointed at me because I was moving in an official vehicle that was blue and it had the police licence plates. It actually was a civilian vehicle, a Fiat Regatta, but it had police licence plates. It wasn't a regular police vehicle with markings "police" on the whole vehicle. This one only had the police licence plates. People didn't know me that much. I had just come to Knin, and this stopover on the road was very short too. My objective was to reach Cupkovica bridge and not to explain anything or to talk with these people, to see what sort of weapons they had. My objective was just to get to the bridge. As for their appearance and behaviour, what I can say is that you could see fear and concern in their eyes. This is what I noticed, that they were really frightened and that this was the main motive why they came to these barricades that they had erected. They appeared to be people who were afraid, afraid for their lives, for the lives of their relatives, their household members, and I assume that that was the reason for those barricades. There was no shooting. There was no other stopping.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You described that compared to other situations, when you would have women and children along the side of the road in the village or walking around, and this time there weren't any women and children. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explain that by again saying that the entire population appeared to be frightened in those settlements. The rule at that time was that in the afternoon, when it got a little bit cooler, when the sun wasn't so hot, the elderly would come in front of their houses, into the yards, and sit in the shade. But at that time, I didn't see them. They probably stayed in their houses. There were no children playing. There was nobody going around about their business. It was a bit tense. Everyone was looking as if they were tense and afraid for their lives. That's why it was foreign me to get to the bridge and see what the situation there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: After you called the Zagreb SUP from Cupkovica Most and said that there had been no incident there, what did you do? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't call Zagreb from there because it wasn't even possible to do that with the equipment that we had at that time. I actually called Knin. I called my station and told the duty operations officer to inform Sibenik and Zagreb, the duty officers in the MUP there, that nothing had happened, and I also told the duty officer that whenever anyone called because there were a lot of calls from the town itself and from other towns he was to say that there had been no clash and that there were no MUP people to be seen. I told him to take steps to calm the situation down. After that, I drove with my people, with this inspector and this civilian, back to Knin because I had a lot to do, to report back, I had to send written dispatches to Sibenik to Zagreb, to organise the service, to wait for instructions and many other things. So I went back to the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And all of this happened on the 17th of August 1990, am I correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what were the developments after that day?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that day, I once again travelled to Sibenik to report on the situation, and I sought a way to resolve this situation, what we were to do in order to reduce tensions because such a situation could lead to an outbreak of conflict, to shooting, to dead, to wounded, to consequences that could not be put right again, to damage that could not be mended. So that is why I went to a meeting there also to report to the secretary and the -- report to the senior officers meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And then what happened after the 17th of August? Did you go and see what the situation was?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to the barricades because there were no directives from Sibenik for the police to go to the barriers, unless there was an incident, that this would be resolved in a different way. I did have to pass through barricades on my way to Sibenik and I saw that they were more firm, they were more dug in, they were larger and then you could even see some military weapons. It wasn't that frequent but you could see the odd army rifle, semi-automatic, and other weapons amongst the people at the barricades, that they did have such weapons. I didn't stay long at the barricades. They didn't know me. I, of course, introduced myself and -- of course, had I introduced myself maybe they wouldn't have believed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were there any policemen at those barricades, any officials from the Knin public security station? I'm thinking of the day of the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: (redacted) This went on for quite a while. The barricades were also under the monitoring of the intelligence services of the Republic of Croatia and the federal such organs and I was never told that there were any policemen at these barricades because I assume that the people in Sibenik knew what was going on and I assumed that the police officers kept their distance from these barricades and had nothing to do with them unless there was an incident or somebody reported that there had been some harassment there or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the beginning of this answer by the witness, I think that the witness said what his post was. Perhaps that sentence would need to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May page 74, line 21 to 24 -- well, to 25, the end of that sentence, may that please be deleted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Whiting is on his feet, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour. I think the last question -- I believe it misstated the evidence. Counsel said that "the police staff of the Knin public security station did not take part in the activities of the barricades because that's what the orders were." And I don't believe that it's the testimony of the witness, unless I missed that. I did -- of course, he has testified that the police did not take part in the operation of the barricades but I don't believe he testified that it was because that's what the orders were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it would be the best thing for the witness to -- I'm just responding to the objection by the Prosecutor. I understood it. The witness explained that the public security station staff where he was did not take part and were not at these barricades and that's how it was for as long as he was at the post that he was at. He also explained what the Sibenik position was on that, the SUP Sibenik public security station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... they just didn't take part but he has never told us about orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that I misunderstood the witness, but the sentence that the witness said, and I just want to explain my position. He said that from the point of view of the person at a certain post at that security station. He said that for as long as I was there, things like that did not happen. This is why I put the question in the way that I did. Nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me tell you what this witness said. This is starting at line 21 of page 74. "The 17th, in the afternoon, when the barricades started cropping up and on the 18th and not during the entire

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us whether you reported your superiors about the situation?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would report to my superiors every day and along with that I informed Sibenik as well as the MUP administration in Zagreb about all the events that were taking place at that time, as well as all the events that took place later in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say that you informed the SUP in Sibenik and the Ministry of Interior in Zagreb about all events, does that include the barricade situation? Did you inform them about that as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards the barricade situation, we informed them as to the total number of barricades which we, as the police, were able to register. It was our task to register the barricades and the complaints of particular citizens who may have complained that they were mistreated at these barricades or that something happened to them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember how many of these barricades there were, Witness?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't visit them all. They were on different roads leading in different directions. However, to the best of my knowledge, they were erected on all the main roads leading to and from Knin. The barricades were also erected in small villages and hamlets in the interior where people set up check-points on their own initiative, although they had no borders with Croatia villages or the Croatian population and although there was no possibility of MUP units passing through. People would simply set up a check-point, man it, then abandon it, but they were constantly there on these main roads leading towards Vrlika and Sinj and then on the road leading to Drnis-Knin, Drnis-Oklaj, on the road to Kistanje, Knin-Kistanje, also the Knin-Gracac road, the Knin-Strmica road, leading in the direction of Grahovo, all the main communications leading to and from Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question simply was are you able to estimate how many there were of these barricades? Can you just give us a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, seven or eight main barricades, those on the main roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And how many minor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's all relative. Whatever I say, I can't be sure of the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The minor ones would have been many more, I'm sure there would have been many more minor roads than main roads. I'm not quite sure what you mean by that gesture. It doesn't get on to the record so you've got to say something verbally so that it goes on to the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I too assume there were many more minor ones but I didn't see them. I assume there were more, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, please tell us whether you informed the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia about everything you have just told us and whether you received any reply from them.

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, we informed both the SUP in Sibenik and the MUP in Zagreb about the situation on a daily basis. We reported more frequently if something happened. We would report any incidents straight away. In September, I think, we were given instructions to do everything possible to reduce the tensions at these barricades because at that time there was a large sports event being held in Split, the European swimming championships. These were being held in Split in September 1990, and Croatia as the host country did not wish these barricades and tensions to spread because this would have affected Croatia's popularity. Therefore, the order was not to take any measures, to let the situation calm down by itself, and we had to get involved only in cases of major incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, were there any incidents at the barricades and what was your response? Can you tell us something about this?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there were some incidents at the barricades. One of the major ones was when a patrol of the public security station from Drnis in which there were three policemen who were all inexperienced because they were new to the station, were on patrol in their area, and they approached a barricade at rather high speed, and this barricade was on the Knin-Oklaj road, after the village of Vrbnik. Somebody fired a shot from the barricade and when the policemen saw that they had come too close, they tried to turn the vehicle and turn back but somebody fired a shot and wounded one of the policemen. The others ran out of the car and took shelter in some nearby houses. A police patrol arrived from Knin, found them, and brought them to the Knin hospital where they were given medical assistance. The injured policeman was hospitalised in Knin and the other two, who had not been injured, were taken back to the barricade and then back to Drnis. I saw them in the hospital. I was there while the injured one was being given assistance. And while this was going on, some citizens broke the windows of their vehicle and took the automatic rifles that were in their vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was this an official police vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was marked with the word "Milicija." It was an official vehicle and they were official weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We spoke about the events on the 17th and the 18th of August 1990 in Knin. In this period, was there anything happening in the Drnis police station?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the precise date. I know it was a few days after these events in Knin. It might have been in late August, around the 25th of August, as far as I can remember. And at that time, there was a rebellion in the police station in Drnis. In the evening, an order was issued that the entire active-duty police force should assemble and the reserve policemen were called to the station. At that meeting, the secretary of the SUP, Bujas, addressed the policemen and issued the order that all telephones be plugged out in the station, and he said that a decision had been reached that the civilians on the barricade on the Drnis-Knin road should be disarmed. This was near the village of Tepljuh. At that point, as I heard, because I was not a participant in these events, the police rebelled. They said they were not ready to carry out this task. They said that quite a large number of people could be killed or injured. They suggested that this action be postponed, that it be carried out in daytime, and they felt the situation could be resolved in a different way. There was an exchange of words. Orders were issued. Orders were refused. At one point, all the policemen put down their weapons on the table and said they were not going to go into action.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As we are coming towards the end of today's session, just one more brief question for today. What was the ethnicity of those policemen in Drnis?

utterances.speaker: RATKO LICINA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in all police stations all over Croatia, the ethnicity was mixed. In Drnis, there were Croats, Serbs and Muslims in the public security station, as well as those who declared themselves to be Yugoslavs. It was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we've already overstepped our time by two or three minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have indeed. We'll take an adjournment and come back on Monday at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, the same court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll come back at quarter past 2.00 on Monday, in the same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 21st day of August, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
